sentences.text: From question to publication with the Shimmer 3 G S R plus: arousal and heart rate during two commercials
This workshop follows one advertising question from a client's first sentence to a written results and discussion section.

You will plan a test of two television commercials, build it in iMotions Lab 11 point 1, place a Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit on a viewer's hand, turn a skin signal into counts of arousal events, test three hypotheses, and write the result for a journal and a client.
Every section explains why before how.
Skin conductance is how easily a tiny electrical current passes across the skin; its other names are galvanic skin response (G S R) and electrodermal activity (E D A).
The sweat glands of the fingers are controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, the branch of the nervous system that readies the body for action.

When something arouses a person, the glands fill, and the skin between two finger electrodes conducts better, a change that "is controlled on an entirely subconscious level," in the iMotions introduction's words.
The unit is the microsiemens (microsiemens), one millionth of a siemens.
The signal has two parts.
The tonic part is a slow level that drifts over minutes and differs widely between people, the skin conductance level (S C L) of research papers.

The phasic part is a set of quick rises on top of it, each a skin conductance response (S C R) in papers and a G S R peak in iMotions, "a biological indicator that something relevant happened at that moment."
A peak arrives late, because the brain's command must reach the glands and the sweat must rise; this latency puts a peak one to a few seconds after its cause.
The study counts Peaks Per Minute, the number of peaks divided by the minutes of usable signal.

The unit also has a channel for photoplethysmography (P P G), or blood volume pulse (B V P): light shone into a finger changes with each heartbeat, and iMotions shows "a continuously calculated beats per minute value" (beats per minute).
Two limits run through every section.
Skin conductance shows the intensity of arousal, how activated a person is, not its valence, whether the feeling is pleasant; a rise can come from enjoyment, surprise, or irritation.
And with no electrocardiogram (E C G), the lab reports mean heart rate only, never heart rate variability (H R V), because "P P G signals are not recommended for H R V analysis."
The lab owns two Shimmer 3 G S R plus units, each with one skin conductance channel and one P P G channel (Shimmer, n.d.)
, streaming over Bluetooth, a short range radio link, to a lab computer, where the G S R R Notebooks, analysis scripts built into iMotions, find the peaks.
The worked example is the lab's "Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation" and "E L F
Campaign Ad Evaluation" studies, with a simulated data set of 30 respondents.
Time needed.
About 4 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (question, design, example, build, collect) in the first, 06 to 10 (methods, numbers, analysis, writing) in the second
Equipment.
A Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit with its two finger electrodes and the optical pulse probe, the lab computer with Bluetooth, and hand wipes
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1 with the G S R R Notebooks, plus R or Excel for section 08
Data files.
The simulated arousal test files in the site's data folder (peak metrics, signal quality, peak table, heart rate, survey, session log, analysis dot R, the Excel workbook), plus the Nike and E L F
Campaign Ad Evaluation studies in the lab Library, opened in class
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need a lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1, one Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit with its electrodes and optical pulse probe, and this page.
You do not need Workshops 1 to 3 or any experience with iMotions.

The statistics you need are a mean (an average), a standard deviation (how far a typical value sits from the mean), and the idea that a test asks whether a difference is larger than chance would produce.
Every other term is defined where it first appears, and terms with a dotted underline open a one line definition when you tap them.
The help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com.
For a longer introduction before section 04, read the iMotions pocket guide to galvanic skin response.
At a lab computer, open iMotions in another window to follow the screens in sections 04, 05, and 07.
Nothing in this workshop records into, deletes, or changes the lab's existing studies; open the Nike and E L F
Campaign Ad Evaluation studies only to look.
The one sentence this workshop keeps repeating Write the exclusion rule and the nonresponder definition before the first respondent sits down.

Every skin conductance study loses some recordings to loose electrodes and Bluetooth dropouts, and some people show almost no peaks whatever they watch; a rule written after seeing the data is a rule chosen to get a result.
Say what skin conductance and P P G heart rate measure and what they cannot, what a G S R peak is and why it arrives late, and which equipment, software, and files this workshop uses.
From idea to research question
A client rarely arrives with a research question.
A client arrives with a business question, a statement of what the business wants to know.
Picture an advertising team holding two finished commercials, one for Nike and one for E L F
, that asks (a teaching scenario, not a statement about either brand): "Which of our commercials gets people more worked up?"
The sentence names a comparison and a feeling, but not who will watch, what "worked up" means, how it will be measured, or what difference would count.
A research question names the problem the study will answer and signals the type of study needed.
A hypothesis is a testable answer to it, written with the variables that will be measured.
First, though, you need to know what a sensor on the fingers can say about being worked up.
Emotion researchers describe a feeling along two separate dimensions.
Arousal runs from calm to excited: how strongly the body is activated.
Valence runs from unpleasant to pleasant.
Fear and delight are both high in arousal and opposite in valence.
The iMotions introduction to facial expression analysis draws the two as a map, arousal from G S R on the vertical axis and valence from facial expressions on the horizontal one.
These two dimensions are the core of the emotion probe framework.

When people viewed emotional pictures, skin conductance rose more for highly arousing pictures whether they were pleasant or unpleasant, and a review of emotion measures concluded that autonomic measures such as skin conductance follow arousal better than valence.
What skin conductance can answerDid arousal rise during a commercial, compared with the same person at rest a minute earlier?
When in the commercial did the peaks gather?
Which of two commercials produced more peaks per minute in the same viewers?
What it cannot answerDid viewers like the commercial?
Which emotion did they feel: joy, surprise, or irritation?
Will they remember the brand or buy the product?
Each needs another measure: a rating, facial expression analysis (Workshop 3), or a criterion such as recall or choice.
The iMotions introduction to E D A/G S R states the limit plainly: G S R shows whether there is an emotional response and how intense it is, but "it does not measure the valence."
It adds that the response reflects "familiarity and prior associations with the stimulus," so a well known brand can move the signal for reasons outside the commercial.
Reading a specific mental state, such as liking, straight off a physiological signal is called reverse inference, and reviews of consumer neuroscience warn against it.
More peaks during one commercial means more arousal during it, and nothing more.
Why measure arousal in advertising at all?
One study related the arousal and valence of television messages to viewers' cognitive capacity and memory (A.
Lang, Dhillon, and Dong, 1995); another examined how message valence and listener arousal affect attention, memory, and facial muscle responses to radio advertisements.
Reviews cover how to interpret skin conductance and heart rate in media research and 20 years of emotion measurement in advertising.

One test compared skin conductance, heart rate, facial muscle activity, and self reports on the same television commercials, and a comparison of six kinds of measures, from self reports and biometrics to brain imaging, as predictors of how ads performed in the market found that they did not add equal value (Venkatraman and colleagues
Arousal is one piece of evidence, not a forecast of sales.
Now the hypotheses, written before any data exist.

The independent variable is what the researcher changes: the period, either a resting baseline (a neutral 60 seconds period recorded just before each commercial) or the commercial, and the commercial itself, Nike or E L F
The dependent variable is what is measured in response: Peaks Per Minute for arousal, and mean heart rate in beats per minute.
Peaks Per Minute is higher during each commercial than during the baseline that precedes it.
Peaks Per Minute is higher during the Nike commercial than during the E L F commercial.
Mean heart rate during each commercial differs from mean heart rate during its baseline, and the change differs between the two commercials.
Exploratory.
Self reported arousal, rated after each commercial on a 1 to 9 scale, is related to Peaks Per Minute in the same commercial.
A two tailed test asks whether two means differ in either direction; a one tailed test looks only in the predicted direction and is blind to a difference the other way.
All the tests here are two tailed, but the hypotheses differ in whether they state a direction.
H1 states one for a reason: a commercial is made to engage, and a baseline is made to be dull.

H2 states one because the team in the simulated plan predicts more peaks for Nike; a real study must write down the reason, drawn from the commercials themselves, before any data exist (open the two studies on the lab computer and ask whether you would predict the same).
H3 states no direction, because the heart is pulled two ways.
Arousal tends to speed it, and attention tends to slow it: when a person turns toward something new and takes it in, heart rate often falls for a few seconds, the orienting response (P. J.
Lang, 1995), and advertising studies have measured attention this way.
Nothing known beforehand says which pull will win.
The exploratory analysis tests no prediction; it describes how well self reports match the skin.
Now the client's sentence can be rewritten.
The lab asks every study to pass through one sentence with four slots: who, sees what, measured how, compared against what.

Here: adult viewers (who) watch both commercials on the lab monitor, each after its own 60 seconds baseline, in an order balanced across viewers (sees what), while a Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit records skin conductance and an optical pulse and a short questionnaire asks how aroused they felt and how much they liked the commercial (measured how), and each commercial is compared with the same viewer's baseline and with the other commercial (against what).
Weak questions about arousal fail in their own ways.
"Which commercial is better?"
asks for a judgment the sensor cannot make: better at what?
"Did viewers love the Nike commercial?"
asks about valence.
"What did people feel?"
asks which emotion, and a peak carries no label.

The repair names an observable, a measure, and a comparison: "Among the same viewers, does each commercial raise the number of skin conductance peaks per minute above the viewer's own baseline, and is the rate higher during the Nike commercial than during the E L F
commercial?"
It claims more arousing, not better.
The last step is to choose one primary measure for each hypothesis before the data exist and to label everything else secondary or exploratory.
The iMotions design guide gives the reason: "Biometric measures are granular enough that you can almost always find some result."
The G S R notebooks give a peak count, a rate, and an average amplitude for every respondent and stimulus, plus a moment to moment curve; test them all and something will come out by chance.
Here the primary measures are Peaks Per Minute for H1 and H2 and the change in mean heart rate (commercial minus baseline) for H3.
Write them into a dated plan.
Filing that plan before collection is called preregistration, and it lets a reader tell a prediction from a story told afterward.
Section 08 holds you to it.

Turn a client's question about getting people worked up into a testable research question, separate arousal from valence, say what skin conductance can and cannot support, and write three hypotheses with one primary measure each, with no direction where none can be defended.
Designing an arousal study
An arousal study is designed around one fact: people differ enormously.
One respondent's tonic level, the slow resting level of skin conductance, can be several times another's, and one may produce a peak every few seconds while another produces almost none.
In a between subjects design, where each person sees one commercial, those differences would be mixed into the comparison.
In a within subjects design every respondent sees every condition and serves as his or her own control.
Each commercial also gets its own baseline, a neutral 60 seconds period just before it, so H1 asks how far each person's rate rose above his or her own rest.
The share of the variance that belongs to stable differences between respondents is the intraclass correlation (I C C).
In the simulated data of section 08, a respondent's Peaks Per Minute in a baseline and in the commercial after it correlate at r equals point 5 0 for Nike and point 5 7 for E L F
, and the I C C of the model for the two commercials is point 4 7 5, almost half (all simulated).
The price of showing both commercials to one person is that the first can change how the second is received.
Carryover is what the first condition leaves behind: tiredness, a mood, knowledge of what the session holds.
Skin conductance adds habituation: responses tend to shrink as stimuli repeat over a session.
An order effect is a difference caused by position alone, such as fewer peaks in whichever commercial comes second.
Counterbalancing shows each order to equal numbers of respondents so that, in the iMotions design guide's words, these effects "would cancel each other out when results are aggregated."
Group A sees the Nike sequence first; Group B sees the E L F sequence first.
The 2 minute rest between the sequences lets the signal settle, but it cannot erase what the first commercial taught or undo habituation.
If every respondent saw Nike first, a rest of any length would leave Nike in the fresher position, and H2 would mix the commercial with its order.
Length matters for a rate.
Peaks Per Minute divides a whole number of peaks by the minutes of signal, so the shorter the window, the bigger the step between values.
In a 60 seconds window each peak adds 1 peak per minute.
In the 30 seconds E L F
commercial of the simulated plan each peak adds 2, so the kept respondents scored 0, 2, 4, or 6 but never 3.
In a 15 seconds Recovery, the short period after each commercial, each peak adds 4.
Timing adds a second problem: because of latency, a peak arrives one to a few seconds after its cause, so responses to a commercial's last seconds land in the Recovery.
So the baselines last 60 seconds, long enough for a steady resting rate; commercials are compared only as rates, never as raw counts; and Recovery values are described, never tested.
The manuals set no baseline length; the iMotions Sony Bravia demonstration study used 1 minute videos of fish on a coral reef.
The simulated study runs two respondents at a time, each with a Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit at its own seat.
A second unit may read slightly differently or hold its Bluetooth link less well.

So keep the unit constant for each seat (Seat 1 always uses the unit named Shimmer 3, unit 8 9 5 6 in iMotions; Seat 2 the second unit, called Shimmer 3 B in the files until its real name is verified), log the seat and unit of every respondent, and compare the devices before pooling them (section 08); section 10 explains why a real study also swaps the units between the seats on a schedule set in advance.
Seat the respondents so that neither sees the other's screen, and ask both not to talk.

The manuals state no settling time after the electrodes go on, so the lab sets a rule: a warm up of 5 minutes with the electrodes attached before the first baseline, with the actual minutes recorded in the session log.
Two kinds of loss are certain.
The first is technical: a loose lead, a Bluetooth dropout, a restless hand.

The G S R Signal Quality notebook reports the Signal-to-Noise ratio (S N R) in decibels (decibels), a ratio of the slow changes that carry the response to the faster changes treated as noise, and Signal missing, the percentage of the stimulus with no data.
The second kind is not a fault.
Some people show almost no phasic activity, the quick rises that become peaks, whatever they see.
Such a person is a nonresponder, and about one person in ten falls in this group.
Write both rules before anyone is recorded.

The exclusion rule: exclude a respondent whose S N R is below 0 decibels, or who has more than 20 percent of the signal missing, in either commercial (0 decibels is the help article's line for poor; 20 percent is the lab's own threshold).
The nonresponder definition: Has Peaks equals 0, no peak at all, in at least 4 of the 6 stimuli.

Nonresponders stay in the main analysis, because an absence of phasic activity is a physiological result, not a recording fault; a second analysis without them shows whether any conclusion depends on them.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real; the usual target is 80 percent.
The paired t test works on each respondent's own difference, and its effect size is d z, the mean of the differences divided by their standard deviation.
In plain words.

For a large effect, d z equals 0.8, a paired test at two tailed alpha point 0 5 and 80 percent power needs 15 usable respondents; a medium effect, d z equals 0.5, needs 34; a small one, d z equals 0.3, needs 90.
The same calculation in G*Power Means: difference between two dependent means (matched pairs), two tails, d z equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power point 8 0: total sample size 34.
G*Power is the program most researchers cite.
The labels small, medium, and large were written for group differences, a rough guide for d z.
The table counts usable respondents, so allow for the losses: about 10 percent for nonresponders, who add almost no change and so dilute the effect, and 5 to 10 percent for signal losses.
The losses are a share of everyone scheduled, so divide the usable number by (1 minus the expected loss) and round up; adding 15 to 20 percent of the usable number falls short.

For a medium effect, 34 divided by 0.85 equals 40 and 34 divided by 0.80 equals 42.5, so schedule about 40 to 43; for a large effect, 15 divided by 0.85 equals 17.6 and 15 divided by 0.80 equals 18.75, so 18 to 19; for a small effect, 90 divided by 0.85 equals 105.9 and 90 divided by 0.80 equals 112.5, so 106 to 113.
The iMotions design guide recommends "20-60 people in each study condition for adequate statistical power."
Two commercials are two stimuli, two specific things shown to respondents, not a sample of commercials.
A difference between them belongs to everything that differs at once: brand, length, story, music, pace.
The result can say that the Nike commercial, as made, produced more peaks per minute in these respondents than the E L F
commercial, as made; a claim about kinds of brands or lengths needs many commercials analyzed as a sample, called stimulus sampling.
Last, consent and comfort.
Explain the sensors first: two finger electrodes carrying a low constant voltage, and an optical probe.

Informed consent is a documented explanation, given before participation, of the purpose, the right to stop at any time, how the data will be handled, and the risks; here it names skin conductance and heart rate as the signals recorded.
The iMotions sanitizing guidance says to "use disposable electrodes," to disinfect with "at least 70 percent alcohol," and notes that G S R and P P G "can be self-applied with instructions."
The N M S B A code of ethics sets out participant rights for commercial studies (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n.d.)
At Jacksonville State a study that will be published or presented first goes to the Institutional Review Board (I R B), the committee that reviews research with human participants.

Defend a within subjects design with a baseline for each commercial, explain why counterbalancing and not the rest protects the comparison, say why short windows give coarse rates, and fix the seats, warm up, exclusion rule, nonresponder definition, sample size, and consent in advance.
The worked example in full
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page, the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the arousal test as a student study plan; read it as a template for your own.

Among adult viewers, does each of two commercials, one for Nike and one for E L F, raise skin conductance arousal above the viewer's own resting level, which raises it more, and how does mean heart rate change during each?
H1: Peaks Per Minute is higher during each commercial than during its own baseline.
H2: it is higher during the Nike commercial than during the E L F commercial.
H3: mean heart rate changes from baseline during each commercial, and the change differs between the commercials.
Exploratory: self reported arousal and Peaks Per Minute in the same commercial.
All tests two tailed.
Within subjects, every respondent sees both sequences.
Two orders for counterbalancing, Group A (Nike first) and Group B (E L F first), allocated alternately from a list prepared before collection.
For each commercial: Baseline (60 seconds), the commercial, Recovery (15 seconds), a short questionnaire; a 2 minute rest between the sequences.
In the simulation: Baseline Nike, Nike Commercial (60 seconds), Recovery Nike, Baseline elf, E L F Commercial (30 seconds), Recovery elf.
Two respondents at a time.
Seat 1 uses Shimmer 3, unit 8 9 5 6; Seat 2 uses the second unit, Shimmer 3 B in the files (a placeholder name; verify on the lab laptop).
A unit never changes seats.

A sampling rate (samples per second) of 128 hertz, which the iMotions Shimmer article calls "sufficient" for G S R, set to the same value on both units and read in the Shimmer settings before each study day.
Heart Rate (the P P G channel) on.
A warm up of 5 minutes before the first baseline (a lab rule; the manuals state none), with the actual minutes logged.
30 respondents scheduled (P 01 to P 30), 15 per order.
G S R Peak Metrics, per respondent and stimulus: Peaks Per Minute, Has Peaks (1 if the stimulus holds at least one peak, otherwise 0), Peak Count, Average Peak Amplitude (microsiemens).
G S R Signal Quality: Signal-to-Noise ratio (decibels), Signal missing ( percent).
Heart: mean P P G beats per minute over each stimulus.
Questionnaire: self reported arousal (1 to 9) and liking (1 to 7) after each sequence.
Exclude a respondent with an S N R below 0 decibels, or more than 20 percent of the signal missing, in either commercial; record the reason in the session log.
A nonresponder has Has Peaks equals 0 in at least 4 of the 6 stimuli; kept in the main analysis, removed in a sensitivity analysis.
H1: a paired t test of each commercial against its baseline, with d z and its 95 percent confidence interval, checked by a Wilcoxon signed rank test.
H2: the same test of Nike against E L F

, plus a mixed model with commercial, order position, their interaction, and a random intercept for each respondent, with the I C C. H3: paired t tests of each heart rate change and of the difference between the changes.
Exploratory: a correlation of self reported arousal with Peaks Per Minute.
Also: H1 and H2 without nonresponders, a device check before pooling, and the percentage of respondents with a peak per 5 seconds bin.
Alpha point 0 5.

A table of Peaks Per Minute and heart rate by stimulus, three figures, a results section and a discussion in journal form, and a three sentence client summary that says "more arousing," never "better."
Four names return in section 08.
The Wilcoxon signed rank test checks a paired t test with the ranks of the differences, sensible for whole peak counts.
The mixed model is a regression that knows which rows come from the same respondent, and its random intercept gives each respondent a personal overall level.
A sensitivity analysis repeats a test under another reasonable choice to see whether the conclusion survives.
Each hypothesis has one primary measure.
H1 and H2 use Peaks Per Minute, a rate, because the commercials differ in length; a rate puts 60 seconds and 30 seconds on one scale, and Peak Count would not.
Has Peaks defines nonresponders and gives the share of respondents with any peak.
Average Peak Amplitude, the mean height of a respondent's peaks, exists only for respondents with a peak, so it is described, not tested.
H3 uses mean P P G heart rate as a change from its baseline.
Self reported arousal serves the exploratory question, and liking is the valence check that skin conductance cannot supply, described only.
The real material is two studies in the lab's iMotions Library: "Nike Campaign Ad Evaluation" and "E L F Campaign Ad Evaluation."

Each has a 60 seconds Baseline, the commercial, a 15 seconds Recovery, and a short questionnaire, and each records a Shimmer 3 G S R plus unit with the respondent camera for aff decks facial expression analysis (Workshop 3).
That is all this page states.
Open the studies on the lab computer to see the content and length of each commercial, the questionnaire items, and the settings, rather than guessing (if its Library does not list them, ask Doctor
Sciuchetti, because the lab keeps saved copies of both study designs); this workshop reports no data from them.
Wherever a number about respondents appears, it is simulated Every number about respondents, in any section, comes from a simulated data set built in the style of these two studies.
No person was recorded, nothing about either commercial went into it, and no number may be quoted as a finding about the real commercials or viewers.

That leaves 28 respondents, 15 in Group A and 13 in Group B, and three notes keep the nonresponders P 03, P 16, and P 21 (all simulated).
The folder also holds analysis.

Each Recovery lasts 15 seconds, so every peak adds 4 peaks per minute and values jump between 0, 4, 8, and so on.
Because a peak arrives one to a few seconds after its cause, some Recovery peaks answer the commercial's last seconds.
And no hypothesis concerns the Recovery: it shows whether arousal settles, reported as a mean and standard deviation only.

studies, name the simulated file that answers each question and the two layouts that must be verified, and explain why the Recovery is descriptive only.
From sweat to peaks: what skin conductance and P P G heart rate measure, and how to describe them
Every result ends a chain: the Shimmer 3 G S R plus records skin conductance and an optical pulse, R Notebooks rate the signal and find its peaks, and an export counts them.
A methods section describes every link (Boucsein and colleagues
, 2012) in the vocabulary of the handbooks.
Skin conductance, also called galvanic skin response (G S R) or electrodermal activity (E D A), is how easily a tiny current passes between two finger electrodes.

The sweat glands are controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, the branch that readies the body for action; when a person is aroused they fill, and "electrical current flows more readily" (Introduction to: E D A/G S R).
The unit is the microsiemens (microsiemens).

One limit governs everything: skin conductance measures arousal, the intensity of a response, not its valence, whether it is pleasant or unpleasant; the article says G S R "does not measure the valence."
A rise can come from enjoyment, surprise, or irritation.
In plain words.
The signal is a tide with waves on it.
The tonic part is the tide, a slow level that differs hugely between people.
The phasic part is the waves, quick rises over a few seconds after something happens.
A wave that clears the notebook's thresholds is a G S R peak.

The terms in the literatureThe tonic component is the skin conductance level (S C L), a phasic response a skin conductance response (S C R).
The manuals say "G S R peak," never S C R; equating the two is this workshop's inference.

The manuals say "G S R peak," never S C R; equating the two is this workshop's inference.
Because the tonic level depends on the person, the room, and the skin, the study counts phasic peaks against each respondent's own baseline.
A peak also arrives "up to a few seconds" after its trigger (Timestamping and synchronization method).
The manuals set no scoring window for this latency, so a peak marks something that happened a second or more earlier.
The G S R Peak Detection R Notebook, a script run inside iMotions, follows Benedek and Kaernbach (2010), as the Peak Detection and Aggregation article states.
It:
reads the calibrated signal in microsiemens at its sampling rate (128 hertz in this plan);
interpolates gaps shorter than the Gap interpolation length threshold in milliseconds and splits the signal at longer ones;
subtracts a running median of Phasic filter length in milliseconds to leave the phasic signal;
smooths it below the Lowpass filter cutoff frequency [hertz];
marks each peak's start and end with the Peak onset and Peak offset thresholds [microsiemens];
keeps peaks above the Peak amplitude threshold [microsiemens] and longer than the Minimum peak duration in milliseconds.
The manuals state no defaults.
Record each value from the panel before the first export (section 07), keep it constant, and report it.
Note: columns from the Export: R Processed G S R Files article; confirm Has Peaks and N A in a real export.
A rate puts a 60 seconds baseline and a 30 seconds commercial on one scale.
Its denominator is Signal Duration because no peak can be detected during a Bluetooth gap; dividing by Duration would count lost data as calm time.
In the simulated data that would have understated three kept rows by up to 0.415, and the excluded row of P 24 would read 4.000 instead of 6.452.
Short windows are coarse: one peak adds 1 to the rate in 60 seconds, 2 in 30 seconds, and 4 in a 15 seconds Recovery, so the Recovery windows are described, not tested.
The G S R Signal Quality notebook reports the Signal-to-Noise ratio (S N R) in decibels, power below a cutoff frequency against power above it, and Signal missing in percent.
S N R "is always calculated on the signal that is present," so read the two together.
The article states two cutoffs; record the panel's.
The study excluded a respondent with an S N R below 0 decibels or more than 20 percent missing (a lab threshold) in either commercial.
Kept S N R averaged 23.0 decibels (standard deviation 3.3, range 14.5 to 30.6), and 31 of 168 kept rows needed a look (simulated).
The Signal Quality file layout is modeled; verify it on the lab machine.
Some people produce few or no phasic responses even with clean electrodes, a stable individual difference that practical guides show how to recognize.

Electrodes, warm up, and the session
Skin conductance is easy to record and easy to spoil.
Movement and breathing change the trace as surely as arousal does, and nothing in the trace says whether a rise came from the commercial or from a deep breath.

Clean data come from three habits: electrodes where the placement article puts them on a hand that stays still, time for the signal to settle, and a written note of everything that happens while it happens.
Check each seat's unit: charged, the widget at Collecting, the primary LED solid blue (section 04).
Define the live markers.
A live marker is a time stamp the operator adds during a recording by pressing a key.
Define the keys before recording, on the study's Live Markers tab with "Add Marker": one each for hand moved, cough or talk, and lead loose.
You should see the markers listed on the tab.

Defining the markers after the first sessions, so the first respondents have no incident marks.

Lay out the supplies: fresh disposable electrodes, wipes or spray of at least 70 percent alcohol, a strap set for each respondent (the sanitizing guidance says to "avoid re-using any straps or wrist bands across participants"), the consent form, the allocation list, and the session log, the operator's record of each session.
The Sensor Placement article names the volar (palm side) phalanges, the finger segments, of the non dominant hand, which leaves the writing hand free for the questionnaire.

Of the three segments, proximal, medial, and distal, it prefers the distal, the fingertip segments, for "greater responsivity"; Shimmer's guide places the electrodes on the palm side of the medial and distal segments.
The electrodermal publication recommendations ask authors to report the recording site, so the log records it for every respondent.

If the fingertips are callused, use the medial segments, as four rows of the simulated log did, and write down which segments you used.
No skin preparation is needed; the article suggests hand cream only on very dry hands (P 03 and P 15 in the log).

The last word of each name tells you what kind of number it is.
C A L means calibrated: converted into physical units such as microsiemens, kilo-ohms, or meters per second squared.
Analyze C A L signals.
raw means the unit's own uncalibrated numbers.
The lab's export gives their unit as "Index," a count with no unit.
They exist for troubleshooting, not for results.
A L G means algorithm.
The manuals never define it, but the lab's export labels Heart Rate and I B I with the data format "Algorithm": they are calculated from the pulse wave, not measured directly.
G S R: the skin signal.
Analysis "is conventionally done on microsiemens values," and the notebooks in section 07 work from conductance, so G S R Conductance, C A L is the one to watch.
P P G: the pulse.
P P G, photoplethysmography, measures blood volume optically with the ear clip or finger probe; iMotions shows "the P P G signal as well as a continuously calculated beats per minute value."
Accelerometer: movement.
Wide Range Accelerometer X C A L, Y C A L, and Z C A L give the unit's acceleration along three axes, "all with the unit meters per second squared."

Gravity is part of the signal ("approximately 9.8 meters per second squared"), so a still unit does not read 0; in the pilot, with the hand still, the three axes together read about 10.35 meters per second squared, almost all of it on Z. Look for changes, not levels.

The help center uses them to find stretches where G S R "is filled with noise due to movement," and its movement notebook's default threshold is 0.2 meters per second squared after gravity is filtered out.
Which way each axis points on the unit is not stated in the manuals.

If a lead comes loose, press the lead loose key, let the stimulus that is playing finish, and reseat the lead during the questionnaire or the rest, never during a baseline or a commercial.

Stopping the recording at the first problem; the rule written in advance, not the operator, decides later whether the data are used.

What Start Recording shows on the lab computer.
The October 12, 2026 pilot found three screens between Start Recording and the first stimulus.

First, a "Respondent informed consent" window reminds the operator that the study records personal data and that clicking OK confirms consent was collected; click OK only after the signed form is in hand (section 02).

Notebooks and exports: from recordings to Peaks Per Minute
Section 06 explained what the R Notebooks compute; this section runs them and writes the files that section 08 analyzes.
Practice on your own pilot study (exercise 5) and leave the lab's Nike and E L F studies unchanged.
Why.
An analysis is a named selection of respondents and stimuli on which notebooks and replays run and from which exports, files written for other software, are made; the recordings stay untouched.
How.
Right-click the study in the Library and choose Add Analysis.
The wizard runs through SEGMENTATION SETTINGS (the name), SEGMENTATION CRITERIA, Signal Processing, and Select Stimuli.
Segmentation, choosing which respondents enter, includes everyone here, because the exclusion rule needs Signal Quality numbers that do not exist yet.
Apply the rule afterward in the script, as analysis.
R does, or in a second analysis with the csv filter that a legacy article places in Segmentation settings (verify on the lab machine).
You should see the Signal Processing step with its "+" button for adding notebooks.
Common mistake.
Dropping respondents whose traces look odd before any rule is applied.

Each R Notebook is added as an Active flow, one notebook run on one device under a name you choose: click "+" next to Active flows, pick the Shimmer under Devices and the notebook under Algorithm, type a Flow name, and set the parameters.
After the last flow, click Next, select the stimuli, and click Add.
G S R Signal Quality first.
Why first: the exclusion rule rests on its Signal-to-Noise ratio (decibels) and Signal missing ( percent), and the rule should be applied before anyone sees a peak count.
Its one parameter, Frequency cutoff threshold for noise, appears in the article as both "here 1.5 hertz" and a "default threshold value (5 hertz)"; the lab computer shows 5 hertz.
You should see the flow under Active flows.
Common mistake.
Skipping this notebook, which leaves the rule without its numbers.
G S R Peak Detection.
The G S R Peak Detection notebook finds each respondent's peaks (section 06).
The manuals state no defaults for its parameters, and the manual's screenshots disagree: the gap interpolation length threshold reads 4 in one and 4000 in another.
Every Sensor Data export, however, records the values the flow used in its header (7.5), which is how the lab read them when the panel would not open.
Copy every value into the plan before the first export, keep the values constant, and never change them after seeing results.
You should see the parameter list under the notebook's description.
Common mistake.
Writing "default settings" in the methods.
G S R Peak Binned Aggregation.

The G S R Peak Binned Aggregation notebook counts, in each time bin, the respondents with at least one peak; the article gives a Time bin length of 5 seconds and a Time bin overlap of 1 seconds as defaults, and the lab computer shows 5000 milliseconds and 1000 milliseconds.
It "can only be executed together with the execution of the G S R Peak Detection R-Notebook."
Common mistake.
Adding it without a Peak Detection flow.
Select the stimuli and add.
On the Select Stimuli tab, choose the six periods (baselines, commercials, Recovery periods) and untick the questionnaires, whose typing moves the electrode hand.
Processing runs in the Background Jobs window (tabs Job Queue, Completed, and Job Errors), and the status bar counts the jobs next to the Background Jobs button.
You should see the count return to 0 and every job under Completed.
Common mistake.
Opening the replay while jobs are still queued, or never checking Job Errors.

The lab ran this exact analysis on a real pilot on October 12, 2026 (one respondent, one Shimmer at 128 hertz, a 60 seconds baseline, a 30 seconds E L F commercial, a 15 seconds recovery, and a questionnaire).
Each choice below says what was picked on the lab computer and why.
The full explanation of every choice, with the help center article and the published research behind it, is in the lab's guide Analysis Choices Explained, Part 2.
The device.
The Devices list offered two entries: "Shimmer 8956 G S R" and "External Events A P I iMotions System Monitor, Sys Load Meter, version 1."
The second is the computer's own processor and memory log, not a body signal, so every G S R flow runs on the Shimmer.
The algorithm.
For the Shimmer, the Algorithm list on the lab computer offers seven notebooks.
This study uses three of them.
The settings inside each notebook.
Settings decide what counts as a peak, so every value is copied into the plan before the first export, kept the same for every respondent, and reported.
On the lab computer the Signal Quality and Binned Aggregation values could be read on screen.

The two groups of Peak Detection settings, "Preprocessing" and "Peak detection," would not open, so the Peak Detection values below were read from the header of the pilot's Sensor Data export, where iMotions writes every setting the flow used (7.5).
They match the manual's screenshots, although the manual text calls none of them a default.
The stimuli.

The pilot analysis kept the baseline, the commercial, and the recovery, and left out the questionnaire, because typing the answers moves the electrode hand and adds false peaks, and the questionnaire is not a stimulus being tested.
The flow names.
The pilot kept each notebook's name as its flow name; every flow needs a unique name, which matters when two units each get their own flows (7.3).
With both seats' recordings in one study, add a Signal Quality flow and a Peak Detection flow for each unit ("add the notebook separately for each device").
Every Active flow needs a unique name, or the panel warns "Algorithm flow must have a unique name."

For example, name the Peak Detection flows G S R Seat1 and G S R Seat2, the Flow Name values in the simulated Peak Table, and the Signal Quality flows SQ Seat1 and SQ Seat2 (the modeled Signal Quality file also shows G S R Seat1 and G S R Seat2; a real file carries the names you give).
Then add one Binned Aggregation with Multiple device aggregation ticked, since it "is not ticked by default," so that the bins pool both units.

On the lab computer in 11 point 1 the box carries a different label, "Consider multiple device as different respondents," and was unticked with one unit (the panel is pictured in 7.2); test what it does in a two-unit pilot before relying on it.
If the seats were recorded on two computers, the recordings must first come into one study.

The Library's right-click menu offers Merge with another study, which no article in this workshop describes, so test it in the pilot; the fallback is to run the notebooks on each computer and combine the exports in R.
A notebook can also run twice on one device with a second parameter set (iMotions 9.3.12 and later, again with unique flow names), reported as secondary to the planned one.
Why.
No number should leave iMotions from a recording nobody has looked at.
How.
Open the analysis and click Replay.

From the Signals menu, show the Shimmer's skin conductance, P P G, and beats per minute traces and, after processing, the notebook's signals (Tonic Signal, Phasic Signal, Peak Detected, and the others in section 06).

The Markers menu lists the analysis markers G S R Peak Onset, G S R Peak, and G S R Peak Offset (iMotions 9.3.12 and later), the Signals menu holds the metrics box shown in section 06, and Reports gives an HTML readout with the R code, the source of the graph in section 00.
You should see peak markers on the rises of the signal and a regular pulse.
Common mistake.
Blaming a peak on the frame on screen at that instant; a peak follows its cause by one to a few seconds.
The aggregate view shows the binned count.
A respondent scores 1 in a bin that holds at least one peak, however many or large, and the scores add across respondents; the article's example reads "10 out of 29 respondents had a response."
The curve therefore shows how consistently a moment produced peaks across people, not how strong they were, and it lags its causes like every peak.
The moment to moment percentages in section 08 come from this count.

With one pilot respondent, the lab computer's Aggregate view of the commercial listed no signals at all after the Binned Aggregation flow ran, so check the binned result with at least two respondents before relying on it.

Testing hypotheses on the Moment To Moment counts, which pool respondents.

Because Info names the respondent and gives age and gender, a real participant's file is identifiable data and never goes in a public folder; the pilot file is the lab director's own recording, shared in 7.7 with his permission as practice data.

Averaging a whole column, including the minus 1 codes, or computing heart rate variability from this column: "P P G signals are not recommended for H R V analysis."

Data Quality Statistics.
The DataQuality dot T X T file from section 05, filed for the methods paragraph.
What the pilot export showed.
The October 12 pilot is one respondent, so its numbers describe the recording and test nothing.
Its value is in what it taught about reading the file.
Four lessons came out of the file.
First, the Peak Detection settings are in the header, so the methods section can be written from the file itself.

Second, the heart rate column read minus 1 for about 2 seconds of the baseline, and the I B I column reads minus 1 on every row except the one where a beat lands; averaging without removing them gives a wrong answer.
Third, at about 19.5 seconds the skin conductance fell from about 1.8 to as low as 0.2 microsiemens and came back about one second later, while the accelerometer showed no movement.
A published quality rule treats skin conductance that changes faster than 10 microsiemens per second as invalid, together with 5 seconds on either side (Kleckner and colleagues
, 2018); here one step fell 0.64 microsiemens within a single sample, about 80 microsiemens per second.
By that rule the stretch is an artifact, and the one peak inside it, counted the moment the signal returned, is set aside; no other pilot peak was flagged.
Fourth, the commercial's rate equaled the baseline's, and the slow tonic level drifted upward through the session; with one person, neither says anything about the commercial.
The plan for the real study should name its artifact rule in advance, so the decision is never made after the results are seen.

Apply the artifact rule.

Under the rule of Kleckner and colleagues (2018), 17 samples between 19.46 and 20.60 seconds change faster than 10 microsiemens per second (the fastest step is 81.4 microsiemens per second), and the 5 seconds margin around them covers 1,421 samples.
Common mistake.
Deleting the stretch by eye instead of by a written rule.
Rebuild the peak table.
The Peak Detected column marks each peak window and Peak Occurrences its maximum.
You should see 14 peaks; Peak Amplitude equals the rise of G S R Interpolated from onset to maximum in all 14, and one peak, at 20.7 seconds, falls inside the artifact margin.
Common mistake.
Counting every row where Peak Detected is 1, which counts samples, not peaks.
Summarize each stimulus.

You should see 8 peaks in the baseline, 4 in the commercial, and 2 in the recovery, 8.0 peaks per minute in each; 7 baseline peaks (7.0 per minute) after the artifact rule; a mean tonic level of 1.80, 2.05, and 1.97 microsiemens; and a mean heart rate of 79.6, 80.4, and 79.9 beats per minute.

Reading the higher tonic level during the commercial as a finding; the level drifted upward through the whole session, and one person tests nothing.

Writing "default settings" in the methods.
Check against iMotions.
Open G S R Peak Metrics dot C S V and G S R Peak Table dot C S V (the script's step 13 and the workbook's iMotions Check sheet do it for you).

You should see the same numbers: Peak Count 8, 4, and 2; Peaks Per Minute 8, 7.98, and 7.99; Average Peak Amplitude 0.0815, 0.0828, and 0.0703 microsiemens; and the same 14 peaks, with onset and peak times that match to the millisecond.

Look at peak 9. iMotions counts it in the commercial because its maximum came at 60.55 seconds, but its onset, at 59.82 seconds, came before the commercial started at 60.22 seconds, so the response began during the baseline.
Common mistake.
Reading a peak in the first second of a stimulus as a response to that stimulus; a skin response follows its cause by one to a few seconds (section 06).
Try it.
On the workbook's Rules sheet, change the maximum rate of change from 10 to 5 microsiemens per second.
The fast jumps near 42 to 44 seconds are now flagged as well, three more baseline peaks fall inside the margin, and only 4 baseline peaks remain.
The count depends on the threshold, which is why the threshold is written into the plan before any data are seen, and why any other value is reported only as a planned sensitivity check.
